title: Peter Cartwright, the backwoods preacher from Logan County
summary: Raised in Logan County when it was called Rogues’ Harbor, Peter Cartwright was converted at a sacramental meeting in 1801, licensed to exhort in 1802, and rode Methodist circuits for two decades before leaving slave-state Kentucky for Illinois in 1824.
bodyMarkdown:
[Peter Cartwright](/people/#peter-cartwright) grew up in the roughest corner of the Kentucky frontier and spent his long life preaching to people like the ones he knew there. He was [born on September 1, 1785, in Amherst County, Virginia](https://grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Cartwright), the son of a Revolutionary War veteran, and came to Kentucky as a small boy.

## Rogues' Harbor

His father first [rented a farm for two years in Lincoln County](https://archive.org/details/autobiographyofp00incart), on the Hanging Fork of Dix River near Lancaster. In the fall of 1793 the family moved on to the Green River country and settled in Logan County, nine miles south of Russellville and within a mile of the Tennessee line.

Logan County was then known as ["Rogues' Harbor"](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logan_County,_Kentucky). Cartwright wrote that refugees from justice had gathered there from almost every part of the Union, until honest settlers banded together as Regulators. On a court day in [Russellville](/stories/russellville-from-big-boiling-spring-to-county-seat/) the two sides fought it out with guns, knives and clubs, and the rogues held the town. There was no newspaper south of Green River and no mill within forty miles. Sunday, he remembered, was set apart for hunting, fishing, horse racing, cards and dances.

The boy fit right in. His father gave him a young race horse and bought him a pack of cards, and he became, in his own words, "a very successful young gambler," while his Methodist mother prayed over him.

## "Thy sins are all forgiven thee"

The turn came in 1801, "in my sixteenth year." Home from a wedding full of drinking and dancing, he was seized by guilt and dread. He gave up the horse, and his mother threw the cards into the fire.

Months of misery followed. Then [James McGready](/people/#james-mcgready), whose Logan County revivals were among [the earliest camp meetings](https://grokipedia.com/page/Camp_meeting), held a sacramental meeting at his meeting-house about three miles north of the Cartwright place. The crowd overflowed the church into a shady grove, with families camped in their wagons.

On the Saturday evening Cartwright knelt before the stand and felt as if a voice said, "Thy sins are all forgiven thee." The same awakening drew the great crowd at [Cane Ridge](/stories/cane-ridge-meeting-house-and-the-1801-camp-meeting/) that year.

## Exhorter and circuit rider

In May 1802 the preacher Jesse Walker handed him a slip of paper permitting him "to exercise his gifts as an exhorter," signed on behalf of the little Methodist society at Ebenezer. It was the only license he had until his ordination. He was [ordained a deacon in 1806 and an elder in 1808](https://grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Cartwright), married Frances Gaines that August, and became a presiding elder in 1812. For two decades he rode circuits in southern Kentucky and western Tennessee, and he was a delegate to [13 General Conferences](https://history.ky.gov/markers/boyhood-home-1793-1802) of his church.

## Leaving a slave state

In 1823 he rode north to explore Illinois, and in 1824 he moved his family to Sangamon County. His first reason, he wrote, was that "I would get entirely clear of the evil of slavery." A daughter, Cynthia, [died on the journey](https://grokipedia.com/page/Peter_Cartwright). He served two terms in the Illinois legislature, and in 1846 he ran for Congress against Abraham Lincoln, who [beat him 6,306 votes to 4,857](https://grokipedia.com/page/Abraham_Lincoln).

## Kentucky today

Cartwright died near Pleasant Plains, Illinois, on September 25, 1872. His *Autobiography of Peter Cartwright, the Backwoods Preacher*, first published in 1856, is still a vivid firsthand picture of Rogues' Harbor. A state historical marker for his boyhood home, 1793–1802, stands on KY 591 at Adairville, and the map pin marks that spot.
